title: The Quiet Playlist
premise: Gideon Winterbourne, a scholarship student at Ashgrove Academy, has spent two years perfecting the art of being unnoticed. When a group chat called The Quiet Playlist starts sending him songs with lyrics describing events days before they happen, he realizes someone is using him as an antenna for something buried in the school's past. The predictions escalate from pranks to a death, and the trail leads to a cover-up involving the academy's founding families and Gideon's own missing father. To expose the truth, Gideon must sacrifice his scholarship, his closest friendship with the headmaster's daughter Wren, and finally his carefully constructed invisibility—choosing to testify at the winter hearing even though the last song on the playlist predicts it will cost him everything.
about_author: Dominic Delacroix is the pen name of a former boarding school music teacher who spent a decade watching teenagers keep each other's secrets. He writes stories about quiet kids who discover that silence is a choice, not a personality.

chapters.title: Track One: Static
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. We meet him mid-ritual: headphones on, invisible, cataloguing Ashgrove's social hierarchy from the margins. He receives a friend request from an unknown account containing a single song file titled with tomorrow's date. The emotional beat is wary comfort—his invisibility is armor, and something is knocking on it.

chapters.title: The Group Chat Nobody Made
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The song's lyrics eerily match a fire alarm that hasn't happened yet; it goes off at the exact minute predicted. Wren Halloway, the headmaster's daughter and his only friend, notices him flinch. He lies to her for the first time. Beat: the first crack in his controlled world.

chapters.title: Scholarship Terms
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She watches Gideon retreat and investigates on her own, finding that his scholarship contract has an unusual confidentiality clause. Meanwhile a second song arrives, this one describing a student falling from the library mezzanine. Beat: dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: The Mezzanine
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The prediction comes true—Cassian Voss falls, survives, but remembers nothing. Gideon realizes the songs aren't threats; they're warnings. He starts a private investigation, photographing the mezzanine's broken railing. Beat: the shift from victim to detective.

chapters.title: Everyone's Playlist Is Different
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. Gideon discovers four other students received songs—each tailored to their private guilt. They form a reluctant, paranoid circle in the music room. Beat: uneasy alliance; the theme of shared secrets surfaces.

chapters.title: Wren Asks the Wrong Question
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confronts Gideon about his secrecy, and he deflects so badly she starts her own inquiry into her father's files. She finds a redacted incident report dated eleven years ago. Beat: friendship strained by the truth neither will speak.

chapters.title: Track Seven: The Drowned Year
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The next song describes a drowning in the boathouse pond. Research reveals a student, Elias Marsh, died there a decade ago—ruled an accident. Gideon's father, a former Ashgrove teacher, resigned the same week and then vanished. Beat: personal stakes ignite.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.summary: Gideon and Wren's alternating POV. They break into the restricted archive at night and find Elias's file gutted—pages razored out. Someone else has been here recently; a fresh cigarette brand matches Headmaster Halloway's. Beat: betrayal looms; trust between the pair deepens even as the institution rots.

chapters.title: Cassian Remembers
chapters.summary: Cassian's POV. The fallen boy's memory returns in fragments: he saw someone tampering with the railing, someone wearing a faculty lanyard. He's terrified to say who. Beat: fear as a weapon of the powerful.

chapters.title: The Playlist Turns Hostile
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The songs stop being warnings and start being threats—describing Gideon's expulsion, Wren's disinheritance, Cassian's 'second accident.' The unknown account finally replies to him: 'Stop digging or the next track is yours.' Beat: the investigation now has a countdown.

chapters.title: What Wren's Father Knew
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren deciphers her father's coded ledger: the Halloway family helped cover up Elias's death to protect the academy's endowment—and her grandfather was there that night. Beat: identity crisis; her name is the crime.

chapters.title: The Friend Who Wasn't
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon traces the account's metadata to a student: Theo Brandt, the circle's quietest member, whose brother was Elias's best friend. But Theo swears he only forwarded songs he received from someone inside the school. Beat: the conspiracy has layers, and one of them is still active.

chapters.title: Interlude: The Quiet Kid's Confession
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, intimate and slow. He finally tells Wren everything—the songs, his father, the fear that his father did something terrible the night Elias died. She believes him. Beat: vulnerability as courage; the friendship reforged in honesty.

chapters.title: Track Fourteen: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A song predicts a disciplinary hearing where Gideon will be expelled for 'unauthorized archive access.' The trap is set: testify and expose himself, or stay silent and let Cassian's 'accident' repeat. Beat: the cost of truth made explicit.

chapters.title: The Boathouse at Night
chapters.summary: Wren and Gideon's alternating POV. They search the boathouse and find Elias's hidden recordings—a tape proving Elias was killed after discovering the founding families were laundering scholarship funds. The final song on the playlist plays itself: it predicts Gideon testifying, and predicts what it will cost. Beat: resolve crystallizes.

chapters.title: Someone Follows Them Home
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, now an ally, is cornered by the real sender—Assistant Headmistress Corliss, Elias's classmate, who has been using the songs to force someone, anyone, to reopen the case before she's silenced like the others. Beat: the antagonist's mask slips; motives blur.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Headmaster Halloway offers Gideon a full-ride extension, his father's whereabouts, and protection—in exchange for the tape and his silence. Gideon sees his father's disappearance was self-exile, shame, not guilt. Beat: temptation; the theme of justice outside the law sharpened.

chapters.title: Track Eighteen: Everything Is Fine
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, ironic title. The school closes ranks: Cassian recants, Theo is suspended, Wren is sent to her aunt's. Gideon sits alone with the playlist and realizes the last song hasn't finished downloading. Beat: the darkest hour; isolation complete.

chapters.title: The Winter Hearing
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Before the board, Gideon plays Elias's tape publicly, streams it, and names names—sacrificing his scholarship in real time. Wren returns uninvited and corroborates with her grandfather's ledger. Beat: climax; truth spoken at maximum cost.

chapters.title: What the Last Song Predicted
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The final track resolves: it never predicted his ruin—it predicted his father walking back into the auditorium, alive, to testify beside him. The cost was never Gideon's future; it was the end of his invisibility. Beat: catharsis and reversal.

chapters.title: Corliss, Halloway, and the Long Ledger
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Aftermath: Corliss testifies fully; Halloway resigns rather than face charges; the founding families' fund is frozen pending investigation. Wren chooses her own name's meaning over her inheritance. Beat: justice outside the law, imperfect but real.

chapters.title: Track Twenty-Two: Gideon Winterbourne
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, closing. Expelled but cleared, Gideon enrolls at a public school where nobody knows his name—and discovers he no longer needs to be invisible. He makes a new playlist, one song for each person who stood with him, and sends the first track to Wren. Beat: identity claimed; memory honored; hope without sentimentality.
